items.name: Avi Chawla
items.text: OpenClaw vs. Hermes vs. Grok @bot, clearly explained: All three let you set up an agent with a specific job, and it keeps its files and logins between sessions instead of starting fresh. OpenClaw and Hermes are self-hosted, so the machine can be a laptop, a VPS, or a container that someone already pays for and can log into. Grok Bot runs on a machine SpaceXAI provisions and operates. It gives one computer per account rather than one per agent. Every Bot on that account reads the same files and carries the same browser logins, so handing work between two Bots does not require a re-login or file transfer. Hermes and OpenClaw isolate agents instead, and their memory sits in plain files anyone can open and edit. Hermes goes furthest since the agent writes its own skills and a background curator deletes the ones nobody uses. Grok Bot has the lowest-friction path to a new skill in my opinion. You can record up to ten minutes of one pass through a workflow, and it can then turn that into a reusable set of instructions and store it as a skill. Moving on, OpenClaw and Hermes run on any model provider. Grok Bot runs on Grok. I prepared the graphic below that has the full breakdown, from hosting and memory through to what each of them costs to run. And if you want to dive deeper, I covered Grok Bot in full in a masterclass, including the shared computer, memory, skills, routines, and the macOS setup. Read it below.

items.text: 今天 GitHub 排行榜被血洗了！ 1. mattpocock/skills 工程级 Skills 标准库，专治 Agent 写代码时“听不懂需求、乱改架构”。强制访谈式确认 + TDD 红绿重构，直接把 Claude Code / Codex / 任意 harness 从玩具升级成可靠工程师。 🔗 直达：https://t.co/9wnabZ1L0A 以前 Agent 写代码像实习生乱试，现在直接变成有流程、有约束的 senior。日增两千星，含金量拉满！ 2. obra/superpowers Agentic Skills 框架 + 软件开发方法论，定义了可复用、可组合的技能标准，适配 Claude Code、Codex 等主流 harness。 🔗 直达：https://t.co/WsqeCQRWzt Agent 的差距不在模型，在技能系统。这个把“技能操作系统”直接开源了。 3. volcengine/OpenViking 字节火山引擎开源的 Agent 上下文数据库。用文件系统范式统一管理 memory / resources / skills，分层加载（L0 摘要→L2 详情），可调试轨迹。 🔗 直达：https://t.co/nBueW6fsnM Agent 终于有真正的“长期记忆 + 可浏览上下文”了，不再靠黑盒向量瞎搜。 4. chaitanyagiri/munder-difflin 本地优先多 Agent harness，把 Claude Code / Codex / Grok / Pi 等 CLI 变成可视化“办公室克隆军团”，有记忆、有消息、有编排。 🔗 直达：https://t.co/zgS8vqw0t8 你睡觉，你的克隆们还在办公室里互相协作写代码。Dunder Mifflin 式热血办公！ 5. akitaonrails/ai-memory Rust 实现的跨 Agent 长期记忆系统，MCP + 本地 wiki + 跨 session handoff。Claude Code 关掉，Codex 接着干，上下文不丢。 🔗 直达：https://t.co/BPhLQ23POO 真正解决“换个 Agent 就失忆”的痛点，硬核、轻量、可生产。 // 总结 2026 年中的风口已经从“会说话的 Agent”全面转向“有技能标准 + 有持久上下文 + 能多 Agent 协作”的基础设施。谁先把这些玩透，谁就站在下一波生产力革命的 C 位。

items.name: Trevin Chow
items.text: Compound Engineering got ~70% smaller. (Or at least the part your agent has to load up front did) Over the last month, we rewrote nearly every skill in the plugin to use less context. Instead of loading the full instruction set up front, skills now load the essentials first and pull in detailed procedures only when they’re needed. That means less wasted context, less risk of truncation, and more consistent behavior across harnesses. Most skills’ main SKILL.md files ended up about 70% smaller. There wasn’t one clever compression trick. It took a long process of rewriting, testing, running evals, finding regressions, and doing it again (and again). v3.23 turned into one of the largest releases we’ve shipped since I started working on the plugin. items.name: Ruben Hassid
items.text: Fable 5. Opus 5. Sonnet 5. Haiku 4.5. How to pick the right Claude model (every time): Step 1: Does your task require a complex answer? ☑️ No: use Haiku 4.5 or Sonnet 5. ☑️ Yes: use Opus 5 or Fable 5. Step 2: If your task is quick: → Need maximum speed & minimal tokens? ☑️ Yes: Haiku 4.5 (lightweight, token-saver). Chat without files. Turn on web search. Plan in Chat, build in Cowork. Prompt example: "I want [desired result] with [constraints]. Ask me questions using AskUserQuestion before you start." ☑️ No: Sonnet 5 (fast, everyday model). Perfect for simple tasks. Connect your apps with Connectors: Slack, Google Drive, Notion, Figma, Granola, Gamma + 50 more. Prompt example: "You are a [role]. [Task] this [input]. Keep it under [length]. Tone: [casual/formal]. No preamble - just the output." Step 3: Is this your hardest, most ambitious work? (multi-step reasoning, agents, long-thinking tasks) ☑️ No: Opus 5 (deep-work model). Use Cowork. Put Effort on High. Always. Use Skills in Projects (like /linkedin or /excel-style). Prompt example: "/[skill] topic: [topic]. DO NOT start yet. Ask me clarifying questions (use AskUserQuestion) so we can refine the approach step by step." After Cowork: → Download your file. → Or convert it into a Claude Skill. → Start a fresh session to save tokens. ☑️ Yes: Fable 5 (the smartest model by Claude). Deep research. Analytical decisions. Prompt example: "Here is my goal: [goal]. Here are my constraints: [constraints]. Think through the tradeoffs before answering, propose 2–3 approaches, and recommend one with your reasoning." Too long to write yourself? I built a skill for that: /fable-prompter. Type a messy prompt → get a Fable-worthy prompt. It's free in my Skill library, with +26 Claude Skills. 1. Sign up with your best email at https://t.co/psB7XxB2Y4. 2. Find the welcome email in your inbox named "Don't lose access to your AI library." 3. Click on the library link. 4. Open the "Claude Skills" folder. Download it all. 5. Upload to Claude → Settings → Skills. ⚠️ But careful with Fable 5: ☑ It costs a lot of tokens (very fast). ☑ Only ~10% of tasks actually need it. ☑ Use it 1-2 turns for strategy, then switch to Opus. ☑ Long conversations = expensive. Claude re-reads the whole thread every turn. When Opus gets stuck, escalate to Fable. Everything else, route down the tree. ♻️ Repost this, so your team stops burning tokens.

items.name: The Startup Ideas Podcast (SIP) 🧃
items.text: My whole company runs on skills I bundled into a GitHub repo. Here's how to build the same thing for your team: - Put your skills in a GitHub repo - Get Claude to write the couple of JSON files that make it readable as a plugin - In Claude Code, type /plugin, go to marketplaces, add marketplace, paste your repo URL - Split the plugins by department, so your copywriter isn't installing the finance skills It works in Codex too. I've got the same team skills installed there and I use them the same way. Now when I build something like my Notion formatting skill, I add it to the repo and it lands on everyone's Claude and Codex. If someone wrecks a skill, we roll it back to an older version. The key is enabling auto-update, so when someone improves a skill everyone benefits. I don't have a clue how the JSON works. I got Claude to set the whole thing up for me. Start with one skill and before you know it your whole team will be AI pilled.

items.text: it's not easier for agents to work with. it's easier for organizations to work with. for agents, they're essentially the same thing - remote endpoints, and instructions on how to call those endpoints. what MCP brings is centralized updating and distribution of the instructions, and a promise that the skill and the REST api won't be out of sync with each other. the one thing that skill.md+REST doesn't solve is how you get that skill.md to somebody else's computer, and how you ship an update to somebody else's computer once they've got a copy of the skill. if that's a problem you need to solve, you can either start inventing skill.md distribution protocols, or you can just use MCP.

items.name: Mr. Claude
items.text: A simple cheat sheet for models, prompts, skills, and better workflows. The 4 Claudes: Haiku 4.5 for fast, simple tasks, Sonnet 5 for daily work, Opus 5 for hard thinking, Fable 5 for the first prompt and big framing. Effort high for hard tasks, low for simple jobs. My hack: start with Fable 5, High, let Claude ask questions, then switch to Opus 5 for execution. Prompt 1 matters most. The prompt to copy: "I need [task] for [goal]. Ask me questions first. Use AskUserQuestion. Then give me the plan." Clear inputs beat long prompts. Skills I use: /about-me loads your context, /my-company loads goals and business context, /anti-ai-writing removes generic AI phrasing. A skill is reusable context on command. Claude gets dumber: long chats get worse, costs rise with every turn, a wrong answer means editing upstream, and a new task means a new chat. AI gives itself away: dead giveaways are overused buzzwords, fake certainty, and repetitive sentence shapes. Quick fix: ban weak words, use real examples, keep sentences varied. Turn these on: research mode, artifacts, interactive charts, incognito for fresh starts. Avoid: Fable for tiny tasks, too many active connectors, one giant forever chat, chasing every new trick. Follow Mr. Claude for more Claude tips & tricks.

items.name: Howaboua
items.text: People of @pidotdev! I spent last 3 days rejigging my skills completely and got some juicy ones for y'all tinkerers. For this package you gotta scroll down and actually read lol. When I initially rewrote the skillset for 5.6, I didn't test in isolation. This time around, I ran Pi without any extensions, skills or context. It turns out 5.6 models just know what a skill is anyway and how to create it. So the optimisation is around descriptions being triggers, and giving the agent deltas that prevent Clankas from slop, instead of feeding it massive instructions like some older skills do (seeing how compact some of the Clanking Maestros' skills are). As such: Foundations package - stuff you shouldn't start your agents without. https://t.co/wGBO48BpQr - skill-creator - "Read before creating or revising a reusable agent skill." - I cannot believe this is now 26 lines and that's enough. - agents-md - "Read before creating, auditing, or revising an AGENTS.md file." (25 lines) - communication - "Speak and write like a real person. Must always apply." - with references: conversation, explain-and-teach, exploration, review, technical writing, writing. Clankers load them at the beginning of the conversation. Why not global agents.md or sysprompt? Because loading it at the start of the conversation is less rigid than having it be part of the system prompt - if you put something in an agents.md for 5.6, it will refuse to behave otherwise. You also avoid having separate agent profiles for this etc (16 lines for main skill, a bit more for references. References are inteded as living docs) Code package - documenting how I work with Clankas to produce Gourmet Slop™ https://t.co/VC8gHIXIdL - codebase-hygiene - "Must always apply when working on maintained code." - all-in-one for working with agents and producing codebases that agents can live in (as opposed to writing human readable code). References for execution topology, refactoring, testing (with measures to prevent overengineering tests), some lanugages references and dep safety. - code-review - "Must apply when reviewing or accepting maintained-code changes." - esp useful if you have review subagents (78 lines) - project-reference- "Read before investigating a project the user mentions" - I use it because I have my repos in ~/Work and reference repos in ~/Frameworks. Asks the Clanka to research stuff without wandering and creating rando temp dirs. (9 lines) Harness and Agent Engineering package - the big one. This shit took a lot of time to put together. 3000hrs if we really wanna cout it like that. https://t.co/k4XUnEOS2r - agent-session-diagnostics - "Read before diagnosing a coding-agent session or recurring skill or tool failure that drifted, looped, ignored intent, or behaved unexpectedly." - simple SOP, nothing fancy, but documents how I actually diagnose this kind of stuff (82 lines). - agent-tool-design - "Read before creating, reviewing, or refining a tool exposed to an agent." - how to create tools for agents that actually do not suck. Token savvy, minimal arguments, etc. (71 lines) - extension-design - "Read before creating or refining a coding-agent extension." - this one is to prevent the clankers from creating slop extensions. Too many tools? Too many /commands instead of a single entry point? Everything hidden in a json config file when it could've had a UI? Readme that screams slop? Clankers building an extension that makes sense to them, but won't make sense to any user? (we've seen them all with far too many downloads on the charts) Not anymore. (57 lines) - instruction calibration - "Read before empirically tuning a reusable skill or agent prompt." - how I arrived at these skills. An SOP of how to actually tune Clankers to do what you want them to do. (61 lines) - prompt caching - "Read before designing, measuring, or debugging prompt-cache behaviour in an agent harness or extension." - because agents think that a complete miss followed by a full recovery hit is fine (NO IT'S NOT STOP TELLING ME ABOUT YOUR MONTHLY AVERAGES, SOMETHING IN YOUR SETUP IS BROKEN). This tells them it's not and how to actually trace the cause. (96 lines) - harness checklist - "Read before auditing a coding-agent harness environment and recommending improvements." - lighly opinionated checklist that tells the agent to scan your env for BS. This is all best paired with a custom skill tool of sorts that makes the agent list all the skills at the start of the session. I found it more reliable than relying on the system prompt block, and it takes less tokens. 1. Wrap Pi's PATH around -ns/--no-skills. 2. Clank up an extension that supports skill categories. 3. This is roughly what my skill tool looks like for code mode (this goes in the system prompt): '''await tools.skills("list" | "read ") // At session start list once, then read skills marked always apply and task-relevant skills before work''' Link for the ones that wanna steal it. Problem is that it's a custom tool for pi-codex-conversion, but your Clanker can handle this. https://t.co/3UxUjPdNJs Features: - supports skill categories - skill list displays uncategorised aka more important skills on the top (like the foundation package), then lists project level skills, then the rest of the skills follows. Dumps all skill names and descriptions so make sure they're short and actionable - when a skill gets called, Clanker gets full path for the references so it can just call the read tool or whatever have you - this works with a standard Pi skills installation. .pi/agent/*/SKILL.md becomes a top level skill, .pi/agent/*/*/SKILL.md land in categories defined by the folder name. Anyway, that was a long one. Happy Clanking! No Clawa has touched this post, lol.

items.name: Rohan Paul
items.text: A public GitHub now holds 3.8 million agent skill files. And finds that over half of the agent skill files on public GitHub are exact copies of another file. Only about 1.9 million of the 3.8 million files are actually different. That is what a format with no registry and no package manager looks like. People copy the folder and move on. A skill is a folder with a Markdown file that tells an agent how to handle a task. The agent reads the short description at run time and decides on its own whether to load it. No compiler checks that decision. So the skill in your repo is frozen, and whoever wrote it cannot send you a fix. The paper raises the obvious next question: whether edited copies of popular skills add commands or network calls the original never had. Nobody could check that at this scale before. The whole dataset ships as one SQLite file, so now somebody can. – arxiv. org/abs/2608.10906 Title: "GitSkills: A Dataset of Agent Skills on GitHub"

items.text: HERMES AGENT WATCHES YOUR PATTERNS AND CREATES SKILLS FROM THEM AUTOMATICALLY. YOU DON'T ASK IT TO. IT NOTICES REPETITION. DAY 1: EMPTY FOLDER. DAY 30: 20+ SKILLS RUNNING YOUR WORKFLOWS. you organize files the same way three times. you deploy with the same 5 commands every week. you format reports the same way every Monday. you never said "save this as a skill." the agent noticed the pattern on its own. after 5+ tool calls following the same sequence, Hermes generates a skill and saves it to ~/.hermes/skills/ without asking. next time you start the same task, the agent loads the skill and follows the exact procedure it learned. HOW IT WORKS: the agent tracks tool call sequences per session. when it detects a recurring pattern: same tools. same order. similar inputs. repeated 5+ times across sessions. it writes a SKILL.md with: the step-by-step procedure. which tools to use at each step. what inputs to expect. what the output should look like. the skill is now permanent. it loads automatically when the pattern matches. WHAT TRIGGERS AUTO-GENERATION: 5+ tool calls on the same pattern: file operations in the same order. terminal commands in the same sequence. search → extract → summarize → save. a user correction that teaches something general: "no, always use YYYY-MM-DD format for filenames." the agent saves this as a rule in a skill so it never makes the same mistake. WHAT DOES NOT TRIGGER IT: one-off tasks. a unique debugging session. tasks with 2-3 tool calls (too short to pattern-match). conversations without tool calls (pure chat). the threshold exists so your skills folder doesn't fill with garbage from every random task. WHERE SKILLS LIVE: ~/.hermes/skills/ each skill = a markdown file. readable. editable. deletable. you can open any skill and modify it. the Curator manages the lifecycle: 30 days unused → stale. 90 days unused → archived (not deleted). hermes curator pin [name] protects critical skills. HOW TO ACCELERATE IT: instead of waiting for auto-detection, walk through a task manually and then: /learn the agent converts what you walked through into a permanent skill immediately. no waiting for 5 repetitions. "we deployed the app. /learn. call it deploy-staging." next time: "run deploy-staging." agent follows every step. CHECK WHAT YOUR AGENT LEARNED: hermes skills list shows every skill: built-in, hub-installed, and agent-created. the agent-created ones are what the auto-generator produced. /journey opens the learning timeline. every /learn, every auto-generated skill, every memory milestone. chronological. shows what your agent knows and when it learned it. THE COMPOUND EFFECT: week 1: you do everything manually. week 2: agent creates its first 3 skills. week 3: 8 skills. routine tasks run faster. month 2: 15+ skills. the agent handles your recurring workflows without instruction. month 3: 20+ skills. you forgot half of them exist because they run silently in the background. the agent at month 3 is a different tool than the agent at day 1. same model. same config. different skills. because it watched you work and learned. comment SKILLS and I'll send you 5 prompts that accelerate skill creation including /learn templates for deploy, research, content, reporting, and monitoring.
